title: What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach

paper.title: What Outcome RL Buys: Finishing, Reliability, Rarely Reach
paper.abstract: Abstract Outcome RL raises pass@1 but not pass@ k k at large k k ( Yue et al., 2025 ) . But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of 20 20 released RL models ( 1.5 1.5 B to 32 32 B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts. Finishing measures answering before the budget runs out. Reliability measures being right once finished. Reach measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing ( 82 % 82\% at 4 4 k and 8 8 k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most 2.1 2.1 percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked 144 144 physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these, 3.5 % 3.5\% hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base’s samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an 8 8 B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem’s physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL.

Outcome RL, which rewards only a correct final answer, is a standard way to train reasoning models. Its gains are reported as pass@1. Whether such a gain is new knowledge or changed behaviour matters. New knowledge widens what a model can solve. Changed behaviour only helps it use what it already knows. The two are hard to tell apart. Every pass@1 is scored under a token budget, so one number mixes answering in time, answering right and solving new problems. Yue et al. (2025) found that outcome RL adds no reasoning the base cannot already produce. Pass@ k k is the chance that at least one of k k samples is right. Once k k reaches the hundreds, the base scores higher than the RL model. The problems the RL model solves are nearly a subset of those its base solves. Prior work calls this narrowing sharpening ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025c ) . We ask whether RL changes behaviour or knowledge at k = 1 k=1 , the score every report rests on. Finishing in time and being right more often change behaviour. Solving problems the base cannot points to new knowledge. We count a gain as new knowledge only when the base finishes all eight samples on the problem and gets every one wrong. We count any other gain as changed behaviour, since the base either answers the problem right at least once or does not finish every sample. Our first question asks of released models: how much of a pass@1 gain is finishing within the token budget, and is the rest reliability or reach? Every recipe is also trained under a budget. If part of a gain is the model fitting its answer into the budget, comparisons between recipes, or between a recipe and its base, partly measure how long each model writes rather than how well it reasons. We ask the first question of thinking models on physics and math. A bounded second question follows: can training install knowledge the model does not use on its own, when it is supplied? Our main study answers the first question by reading twenty released RL models against their bases at fixed budgets. All twenty start from thinking bases, which distillation has already widened. Yue et al. (2025) leave thinking bases open. Once the budget suffices, reliability rises on physics wherever the base already finishes. Reach stays small. The second question tests the obvious remedy for sharpening: hand the model the knowledge its derivations lack (a hint, a teacher’s derivation, or a question about the setup). We train an 8 8 B thinking model with outcome RL on physics, supplying in five ways the physical setup of problems its base almost never solves. At this small scale, the supplied setup changes the model during training but is not shown to carry over to held-out problems beyond plain RL. Reward raises a problem’s solve rate only once the model samples a success on that problem (§ 5 ). Released recipes that use the remedy, QuestA and KnowRL, reach only a little further. Their net reach is at most 0.018 0.018 (§ 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (1) A budget-aware split of the pass@1 gain into finishing, reliability and reach (Eqs. ( 1 )–( 5 )). Unlike pass@ k k , it separates answering in time from answering right. The split also nets reach against the reverse. (2) A read of twenty released pairs on thinking bases , the case Yue et al. (2025) leave open, at each recipe’s own training cap and the next budget above it (§ 4 ). (3) A comparison rule : compare a recipe with its base at or above its training cap. (4) A controlled probe that supplies an 8 8 B model, in five ways, the setup of physics problems its base almost never solves, and tests transfer to their text-only twins (§ 5 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: What RL with verifiable rewards changes. Prior work disagrees on what outcome RL changes. None splits the measured gain into finishing and the rest. On pass@ k k curves, RL raises pass@1, but the base wins at large k k ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) . RL stays within what the base can sample. Yue et al. (2025) count the problems only the RL model solves at 0 0 – 1 % 1\% on AIME24 and MATH500, at k k up to 1,024 1{,}024 . Follow-ups trace this lost coverage to hard prompts whose rare successes drop out of small sample groups ( Zhou, 2026 ) and to winner-take-all reinforcement of what the base already finds likely ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Others trace part of reported gains to budget mismatch and attempt inflation ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Yang & Chen, 2026 ) . Studies of derivations say RL narrows the policy where fine-tuning broadens it ( Matsutani et al., 2025 ) , acts on a few tokens where derivations branch ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and amplifies habits the base already has ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ) . Power sampling, entropy minimisation and even spurious rewards reproduce much of RL’s gain ( Karan & Du, 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) . One training example recovers most of a full data set’s gain ( Wang et al., 2025d ) . A second RL stage shortens derivations at no cost in accuracy ( Fatemi et al., 2025 ) . Both results say RL moves behaviour more than content. Prolonged training, by contrast, is reported to expand the solvable set ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Decompositions find RL improves execution within a fixed coverage ( Qin et al., 2025 ) . Fine-tuning, not RL, moves knowledge ( Wu et al., 2025c ) . All this evidence is observational: no work supplies the missing content and tests whether RL learns it. Our reliability term is the execution gain of Qin et al. (2025) with finishing removed. We compare reliability with finishing at each budget. Our reach is a term of an exact split of the pass@1 gain, counted per problem at k = 8 k=8 . The base-only count in reach controls for sampling noise. Problems only one model solves are resampled and read. Unlike budget corrections of reported gains ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , we split the gain at a fixed budget. We also read each recipe at its own cap. Objectives, samplers and replay. Other work changes how RL credits rare successes. We use one such method, replay. Pass@ k k objectives reshape the group advantage ( Chen et al., 2025d ; Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . VinePPO branches continuations to estimate credit ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ) . RLEP replays past successes into the group ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Replay shows what reward teaches once a success is sampled. Measuring RL on thinking models. Length and answer rate are known confounds ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2025b ; Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025 ; Hou et al., 2025 ) . For a fixed thinking model, accuracy at a cap rises with the cap ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Any change to derivation length therefore changes the score. We separate the two with the finishing decomposition. We also fix a held-out set before training and measure its noise floor.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental Setup
sections.text: This section gives the study’s scope, the three metrics that split pass@1 under a budget (§ 3.1 ) and the protocol for reading the twenty released pairs (§ 3.2 ). Scope: thinking bases. We study thinking bases because they give RL the most to change: how long the model reasons, when it commits to an answer and how often that answer is right, not only whether it answers. A token budget makes each change visible in the score. Practice uses thinking bases too. The strongest open models on math and science, DeepSeek-R1 and its distills and Qwen3, ship in this thinking mode. Every recipe we study starts from one of them. All models studied are thinking models: the five bases (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B and 7B, Qwen3-1.7B and 4B in thinking mode, OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B), the 14 14 B and 32 32 B bases added later, and our controlled run’s Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking. Models that answer in a few hundred tokens are out of scope, except one pair read for contrast: Qwen2.5-7B and its outcome-RL version, Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B (§ 4.1 ). Scope: physics and math. To tell changed behaviour from new knowledge, we read every pair in two domains. Math is the recipes’ own domain: all twenty recipes we study train on competition math and report math results. A gain on math shows what RL buys where it was trained. A gain on physics shows what RL buys outside that domain. Physics is at most about 1 % 1\% of the RL training data of every recipe that states its mix, except ProRL v2, whose mix includes STEM. Skywork-OR1-Math-7B does not state its mix. Physics problems also need modelling, which math problems rarely exercise. A physics derivation first picks the governing principle and decides which quantities and effects matter, and only then does the algebra. A wrong setup is not repaired by careful algebra later. Once they finish at 16 16 k, the five bases are right on 85 85 – 91 % 91\% of their MATH-500 derivations but only 21 21 – 56 % 56\% of their physics ones. The modelling also makes physics derivations long, so the token budget binds more often than on math (§ 4.1 ). Test sets. Each domain has a main set and a check. The main physics set is 300 300 text-only problems from the training corpus of our controlled run (§ 5 ), so both questions share one audited answer checker. The set keeps only problems the controlled run’s base solves at least sometimes, so pass@1 can move. Filtering on the base caps how much reach can show, so 671 671 unfiltered physics problems check the reach result (Appendix A.6 ). On math, the main set is MATH-500, the recipes’ standard benchmark. The math check is 276 276 recent contest problems, below MATH-500’s ceiling, some released after every model (Appendix A.7 ). We call it competition math. sections.heading: 3.2 Protocol for Reading the Released Pairs
sections.text: We read twenty released outcome-RL models, each against the thinking base it was trained from (Table 6 ). Eighteen are of up to 7 7 B. The other two are a 14 14 B and a 32 32 B pair. Each RL model and its base are sampled the same way, with one prompt and one answer checker, the matcher. Each model writes k = 8 k=8 answers per problem at temperature T = 0.6 T=0.6 . Budgets: 4 4 k, 8 8 k and 16 16 k; the recipe’s training cap; and the next budget above the cap on a fixed grid up to 64 64 k. The split is read at k = 1 k=1 , per sample. fin@1 ( B ) (B) is the share of derivations that finish within B B . pass@1 ( B | fin ) (B\,|\,\text{fin}) is pass@1 on finished derivations. Reach is read at k = 8 k=8 , as reach@8 and reach ≥4 @8 ( k = 32 k=32 in Appendix A.5 ). We registered predictions for ten pairs at 4 4 k and 8 8 k, committing them before any of their outputs existed. Reads at the cap and the next budget above it were not registered.

A point’s vertical distance from the diagonal is the rest of the change: reliability, reach and partial credit. The correlation is 0.99 0.99 at 4 4 k and 8 8 k and 0.92 0.92 at 16 16 k. Outcome RL moves derivation length toward what earns most reward within its cap. The effect on finishing therefore depends on where the base starts. At a short cap, RL teaches a thinking base to fit its derivations inside the cap, as ProRL v2 does at 8 8 k. At a long cap, RL teaches longer derivations. The RL model then finishes less often, as Polaris-1.7B does even at its own cap. Across recipes, the change in derivation length tracks the change in finishing (Table 1 ). RL lengthens derivations on a short-answer base too, and the RL model then finishes less at a tight budget (Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B ( Hu et al., 2025 ) ; Table 1 ). Finishing is not hidden knowledge. A base that cannot finish within B B tokens might not know how to derive the answer. Two results argue against this reading. First, the extra tokens go to hesitation, not derivation. In our controlled run (§ 5 ), RL halves the backtracking words (“wait”, “actually”) per derivation. Reliability on problems finished both before and after training does not move. Second, given more tokens, the base solves most of the problems on which RL, at a tight budget, finishes more often and scores higher. We pick those problems with four of the eight samples, then score them on the other four and on a separate 64 64 k base run. At 64 64 k the base passes the RL model on the problems picked at 4 4 k and closes most of the gap on those picked at 8 8 k (Table 1 ). The gap the base does not close counts as reliability, not finishing. Finishing and knowledge are not fully separable, since committing to the right approach is a skill. Our claim is narrower: RL adds few steps the base does not already write (§ 4.3 ). Finishing still pays at a tight deployment budget, as ProRL v2 at 8 8 k shows.

Matched reliability, measured only on problems both models finish, avoids that pull (§ 3.1 ). With matched reliability, the four recipes gain some reliability as well. sections.heading: 6 Discussion and Limitations
sections.text: The two questions, answered. On the released models, RL’s gain is changed behaviour by our definition, not new knowledge. Where the budget binds, finishing is most of the change ( 82 % 82\% at 4 4 k and 8 8 k). Where it no longer binds, the gain is reliability, from steps the base already writes or from answer form. New knowledge, measured as reach, is rare. At our probe’s scale, supplied knowledge is not shown to transfer beyond the problems reward lands on. ProRL v2, trained fifty times as long as our probe, holds two of the five real physics wins. A much larger scale may matter. What this means in practice. Report pass@1 at a budget together with fin@1 ( B ) (B) at that budget. Otherwise a model that stops sooner will look like one that reasons better. Compare a recipe with its base at or above its training cap. Below the cap, a recipe trained long looks worse than it is. QuestA and the two Polaris recipes score below their bases on physics at 16 16 k and no longer do at their own caps (Table 8 ; 16 16 k cells released). On MATH-500, QuestA still loses 0.07 0.07 at its cap. Limitations. The released-pair study and the controlled run are bounded in scale, sampling and grading, and cover thinking bases only. Each limit below names what we checked. The probe. The controlled run has one seed per treated arm, one model family and one domain. The run’s held-out set was chosen on base-model samples. The channels ran at up to the control’s scale, about two visits per problem. Prolonged training is untested. Supervised distillation at scale, known to transfer ( Yue et al., 2025 ) , is untested too. Sampling. The released pairs are read with eight samples per problem ( 32 32 or 64 64 on lone-win problems). The budgets are three fixed ones, the cap and the next budget above it, up to 64 64 k. Only Polaris evaluates higher, at 90 90 k. The pairs are read at temperature 0.6 0.6 , where nine recipes report at 0.7 0.7 to 1.4 1.4 . The eight pairs re-read at their authors’ temperatures split the same way (Appendix A.3 ). A second generation of 16 16 pairs, three of them cap-bound (Table 9 ), moves each term at the cap by at most 0.007 0.007 , inside every interval. Reach. Our definition counts as behaviour the tenth to third of the gain on problems the base never gets right but leaves some samples unfinished (§ 4.3 ). Filtering the physics problems on the controlled run’s base caps how much reach they can show. On MATH-500, neither model was resampled on the problems it alone fails. The MATH-500 mirror may therefore hold real losses of coverage. On both physics sets, both models were resampled (Appendices A.5 and A.6 ). Physics is at most about 1 % 1\% of the recipes’ stated RL data but may be in the bases’ pretraining. We did not check our problems against any recipe’s training set. Grading. The answer matcher is strict, and stricter for larger models. On the 40 40 reliability problems checked by language-model readers, 12 12 RL wins over the base differ only in answer form or grading. Part of the measured reliability gain therefore reflects which answer forms the matcher accepts. Regraded under the fixed judge protocol of Appendix C.2 , 3 3 – 6 % 6\% of the matcher-rejected physics answers become right for the 1.5 1.5 B and 1.7 1.7 B models, and 10 10 – 17 % 17\% for the 4 4 B to 32 32 B models. On the eight pairs with stored texts and the 16 16 regenerated pairs, the judge raises pass@1 ( B | fin ) (B\,|\,\text{fin}) for base and RL alike. On the 16 16 regenerated pairs, the judge lowers the reliability term at the cap by 0.003 0.003 on average, about 8 % 8\% of it. The judge moves net reach by less than 0.01 0.01 (Table 9 ). Closed models were trace readers (Claude Opus 5.5) and setup grader (Claude Sonnet 5). The trace readings are by one language model. One author checked the model’s claimed new steps. No human checked the step checks’ finds. Only the new-step comparison ( 143 143 pairs) and the step checks were read blind.

sections.heading: A.1 How the traces were read
sections.text: Protocol. We read up to twelve problems per recipe that the RL model solves and its base, despite finishing, does not. Two language-model readers (Claude Opus 5.5) see both derivations with model and grade labels, so the reading is not blind. The readers mark whether the RL derivation states a principle, method or reading the base’s never states. A third reader settles disagreements. Of the 195 195 wins, 42 42 are grading or answer-form artifacts (full table in the released repository). Blind reading. A blind, shuffled re-read of 143 143 pairs asks whether each side states a step the other never does. Weighted to the 195 195 wins, it finds a new step on the RL side in 46 % 46\% and on the base side in 50 % 50\% , assuming the 60 60 unmarked pairs read stand for the other 112 112 . A failed derivation lacks steps as often as the winning one, so the labelled count measures attention as much as content. A human check of the new steps. One author, blind to side, checked the claimed new steps in 50 50 of the 143 143 pairs, drawn at random with a fixed seed. Of 45 45 decided claims ( 12 12 unsure), 19 19 hold. There is no detectable difference between sides: 10 10 of 26 26 for RL ( 0.38 0.38 [ 0.22 0.22 , 0.57 0.57 ]), 9 9 of 19 19 for the base ( 0.47 0.47 [ 0.27 0.27 , 0.68 0.68 ]). The readers overcount on both sides, so the counts above are upper bounds. The symmetry the reuse finding rests on survives. The check tests only claims made, so it gives no κ \kappa . Repertoire check. A step missing from one base sample may still be in the model, so checkers searched four other base samples on the same problem. Of the 83 83 steps flagged in the unblinded reading ( 37 37 from the first eight recipes, 46 46 from the ten added), 77 77 appear in one, 37 37 used correctly. Six appear in none. Two of the 77 77 were found only weakly and no finds were re-examined, so the count may lean toward finding them. Of the 10 10 RL-side steps the human check upheld, the base’s samples hold 9 9 . Of the 80 80 blind RL-side steps, the search finds 58 58 , 32 32 of them used correctly in a base sample that then abandons them. The search misses 13 13 , and 9 9 were not searched because their base samples were not stored. The reverse search gave each blind base-side step on a physics problem, with the same prompt, to a reader with four samples of the RL model from the 16 16 regenerated pairs. The reverse search finds 52 52 of the 62 62 , 15 15 of them used correctly, and misses 10 10 . The regenerated pairs hold no math or e3 texts, so 9 9 base-side steps were not searched. On physics the forward search finds 49 49 of 60 60 . Beyond the verdicts, the reverse readers wrote short reports, which call five of the 52 52 finds borderline. Counting the five borderline finds as misses leaves 47 47 of 62 62 . The forward readers returned verdicts only, so the forward search has no count of borderline finds. The human check took one author one sitting of about half an hour. The same author later checked the 15 15 misses the human check had not decided, blind to side and with the same two questions. Over both checks, the author upholds 2 2 of the 11 11 RL-side steps the forward search misses on physics, rejects 6 6 and is unsure of 3 3 . Of the 10 10 base-side steps the reverse search misses, the author upholds 4 4 , rejects 2 2 and is unsure of 4 4 . The forward search’s two math misses are both rejected. Counting both checks, the other model’s samples hold 9 9 of the 11 11 upheld RL-side steps and 6 6 of the 10 10 upheld base-side steps on physics. Reliability problems. A fresh reader then searched the base’s right and wrong samples for that step. Twelve comparisons had no step to search: the values match, and only form, units, a missing box or grading differs. Of the 28 28 searched, 2 2 claims were judged not decisive. Of the other 26 26 steps, 25 25 are used correctly in a base sample graded right, 1 1 is stated only in a base sample graded wrong, and none is absent. The base’s wrong samples state the step on all 26 26 problems: 17 17 without carrying it through, 9 9 using it correctly and failing elsewhere. sections.heading: Appendix B The controlled run
sections.text: Privileged information for hard groups. Partial solutions ( Li et al., 2025 ; Amani et al., 2025 ) , answer-derived hints ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , scaffolds ( Zhang et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025c ) , reverse curricula ( Xi et al., 2024 ) , hint reweighting ( Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , expert traces ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2025 ) and trained hinters ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ; Liao et al., 2026 ) report the deployed score, not whether content was learned. These methods do not control finishing. Our channels belong to these families and claim no algorithmic novelty. Process rewards ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) need a target step, which on all-fail problems only a reference solution gives. Answer-conditioned rationales ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Phan et al., 2023 ) and hindsight relabelling ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) leak the reward. We supply a setup, not an answer.

sections.heading: B.1 The probe in full
sections.text: The run. The control is Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking ( Bai et al., 2025 ) trained with outcome RL (GSPO; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) on PhysReason ( Zhang et al., 2025d ) and UGPhysics ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Yang, 2026 ) at a 12 12 k-token cap. Each arm adds a channel supplying the setup , the physical modelling before any algebra: a reward, the prompt, hinted derivations, a policy-written setup, or a stronger model’s questions. Two hard sets. The held-out hard set is 87 87 PhysReason problems the base solves at most once in eight, never trained on, frozen before any arm under one registered protocol. A fresh base read scores 0.16 0.16 , above what selection implies, so arms are compared with the control. The training hard set is 160 160 problems the control never solved in its first thirty steps. As in § 4 , the control’s held-out score rises from 0.16 0.16 to 0.26 0.26 almost all by finishing (fin@1 ( B ) (B) 0.39 → 0.69 0.39\to 0.69 ; pass@1 ( B | fin ) (B\,|\,\text{fin}) flat at 0.38 0.38 ). The missing fact is often in the model, which does not ask for it. The right question, without the answer, nearly triples the training hard set’s share solved at least in part in eight samples ( 0.062 → 0.175 0.062\to 0.175 ; gold setup 0.350 0.350 ). A stronger model’s questions written without the reference setup give 0.200 0.200 , so the gain is not only leakage. At 64 64 samples, 41 % 41\% is solved only with help and 34 % 34\% under no condition we tried. The model’s own questions do no better than a generic checklist. No channel raises the held-out score clear of zero. Only a pilot of the reward gave a valid read, since at full scale the policy gamed its scorer (§ B.2 ; Appendices B.6 – B.10 ). The setup hint leads the two control seeds by + 0.009 +0.009 and + 0.019 +0.019 , below the detection floor (Table 14 ). Hinted derivations move it − 0.05 -0.05 , beyond the seed gap. The policy-written setup moves it − 0.03 -0.03 , near the detection floor. A + 2.4 +2.4 -point hint-arm lead on an earlier corpus did not hold at the 16 16 k read. The held-out problems mostly carry figures but are given as text. Content is detected only where trained. The control lifts the training hard set’s pass@8 from 0.056 0.056 to 0.344 0.344 (§ B.2 ). On the held-out set, drawn from another source, the control’s gain is almost all finishing. On the 160 160 easier text-only twins of its training problems it gains mostly by finishing. Content transfer is neither shown nor excluded (Appendix B.13 ). The channels’ failure may therefore not be specific to them. Whether recurring techniques explain why guidance gains on competition mathematics is untested here.

sections.heading: B.6 Channel A: reward the setup
sections.text: The comparator’s milestone reward is inert. The milestone reward’s dense term carries 4.7 % 4.7\% of advantage mass, flips no sign and is zero 96.7 % 96.7\% of the time. Design and result. All-wrong rollouts are rewarded with a frozen judge’s probability that they commit to the setup claims. At one twelfth of the control’s scale every trend is flat. The judge’s AUC there is 0.655 0.655 . Signal-to-noise is 0.65 0.65 against 2.26 2.26 . Caveat: at full scale the scorer was gamed. The rerun learned to append the units the answer matcher required, a + 99 % +99\% apparent gain and no real one. The rerun’s absolute figures cannot be recovered. A powered rerun with a valid scorer was never done.

sections.heading: B.7 Channel B: supply the setup in the prompt
sections.text: The hint helps in context and is not kept. The setup block appears with probability 1 − s / 59 1-s/59 at step s s , so the final policy trains without it. Hinted rollouts lead by + 0.13 +0.13 early and do not lead late. On the 59 59 problems the hint revives, a hinted correct rollout establishes 62 62 of 68 68 contested claims and a late unhinted one 12 12 of 57 57 . On matched data the hint shows no gain. The hint arm is + 0.09 +0.09 [ − 1.38 -1.38 , + 1.75 +1.75 ] over its control (full table in the released repository). The setup hint beats a content-free checklist of the same length only on PhysUniBench-OE ( + 3.9 +3.9 [ + 1.1 +1.1 , + 6.6 +6.6 ]). The PhysOlym-A lead is therefore prompt scaffolding.

sections.heading: B.8 Channel C: distil the hinted derivation
sections.text: Design. When a student group is all wrong, up to k = 4 k{=}4 correct hinted teacher rollouts replace its last rows, rescored under the unhinted prompt. There is no KL anchor or off-context correction. Channel C teaches the problems it touches. Early-spliced problems go from 12 % 12\% to 59 % 59\% fully solved, against 17 % 17\% to 31 % 31\% for never-spliced ones. The setup readout does not change. Channel C ends below the control, and untouched problems get worse. Forced to answer on the held-out hard set, it scores 6.2 6.2 against the control’s 8.1 8.1 , a gap of 1.9 1.9 [ − 0.2 -0.2 , + 4.0 +4.0 ] in the control’s favour. On 371 371 untouched training problems the delta is − 5.1 -5.1 [ − 6.8 -6.8 , − 3.5 -3.5 ], flat across similarity. Outputs run about 15 % 15\% longer. One seed.

sections.heading: B.9 Channel D: make the policy write the setup
sections.text: A self-written block shows no gain. Following TraceLift ( Han et al., 2026 ) , the policy’s blocks give a frozen copy − 0.008 -0.008 [ − 0.054 -0.054 , + 0.040 +0.040 ] over no block, against + 0.050 +0.050 [ − 0.009 -0.009 , + 0.110 +0.110 ] for the gold block. A block the policy can write is one the frozen copy already assumed. Rewarding a written setup section changes the section, not accuracy. A lenient judge was gamed ( 75 % 75\% of claims marked established against a strict grader’s 34 % 34\% ). Under a strict judge held-out hard-set accuracy is 0.202 0.202 against the control’s 0.238 0.238 at 30 30 updates. Within a group, a more complete section does not solve more often ( + 3.0 +3.0 [ − 2.8 -2.8 , + 5.8 +5.8 ]). Most wrong derivations ( 80 % 80\% ) used every reference claim.

sections.heading: B.10 Channel E: distil the questioner
sections.text: Design. We fine-tuned on 210 210 correct base derivations, each opened by setup questions Claude Sonnet 5 wrote. The control fine-tune drops the questions. The habit is learned and inert. The model asks in 99.5 % 99.5\% of samples. Asking samples solve 2.0 % 2.0\% of the time, others 2.6 % 2.6\% . But every pass@1 is scored under a token budget. Every recipe also trains under one. On physics and math problems at fixed token budgets, we compare the pass@1 of 20 20 released RL models ( 1.5 1.5 B to 32 32 B) with that of the thinking models they started from. We ask whether each pass@1 gain is changed behaviour or new knowledge. We divide each change in pass@1 into three parts. Finishing measures answering before the budget runs out. Reliability measures being right once finished. Reach measures problems RL solves that its base answered wrongly in all eight tries, minus problems the base solves that RL answered wrongly in all eight. We find four things. (1) Where the base often hits the token budget before answering, most of the change, gain or loss, is finishing ( 82 % 82\% at 4 4 k and 8 8 k). Given more tokens, the base closes most of the finishing gap itself. (2) Where the base has enough tokens, the gain is reliability: the RL model is graded right more often, even on problems both finish. (3) By our definition, RL rarely solves what its base cannot. Reach adds at most 2.1 2.1 percentage points on any of our four physics and math sets. We checked 144 144 physics problems that only the RL model solved. Of these, 3.5 % 3.5\% hold up when resampled or read. In a random sample, nine of ten new RL steps a human confirmed also appear in the base’s samples. (4) In a small-scale RL run on an 8 8 B model, the gain on new problems is finishing, with reliability flat. Supplying each problem’s physical setup was not shown to improve on plain RL. Outcome RL, which rewards only a correct final answer, is a standard way to train reasoning models. Its gains are reported as pass@1. Whether such a gain is new knowledge or changed behaviour matters. New knowledge widens what a model can solve. Changed behaviour only helps it use what it already knows. The two are hard to tell apart. Every pass@1 is scored under a token budget, so one number mixes answering in time, answering right and solving new problems. Yue et al. (2025) found that outcome RL adds no reasoning the base cannot already produce. Pass@ k k is the chance that at least one of k k samples is right. Once k k reaches the hundreds, the base scores higher than the RL model. The problems the RL model solves are nearly a subset of those its base solves. Prior work calls this narrowing sharpening ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Qin et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025c ) . We ask whether RL changes behaviour or knowledge at k = 1 k=1 , the score every report rests on. Finishing in time and being right more often change behaviour. Solving problems the base cannot points to new knowledge. We count a gain as new knowledge only when the base finishes all eight samples on the problem and gets every one wrong. We count any other gain as changed behaviour, since the base either answers the problem right at least once or does not finish every sample. Our first question asks of released models: how much of a pass@1 gain is finishing within the token budget, and is the rest reliability or reach? Every recipe is also trained under a budget. If part of a gain is the model fitting its answer into the budget, comparisons between recipes, or between a recipe and its base, partly measure how long each model writes rather than how well it reasons. We ask the first question of thinking models on physics and math. A bounded second question follows: can training install knowledge the model does not use on its own, when it is supplied? Our main study answers the first question by reading twenty released RL models against their bases at fixed budgets. All twenty start from thinking bases, which distillation has already widened. Yue et al. (2025) leave thinking bases open. Once the budget suffices, reliability rises on physics wherever the base already finishes. Reach stays small. The second question tests the obvious remedy for sharpening: hand the model the knowledge its derivations lack (a hint, a teacher’s derivation, or a question about the setup). We train an 8 8 B thinking model with outcome RL on physics, supplying in five ways the physical setup of problems its base almost never solves. At this small scale, the supplied setup changes the model during training but is not shown to carry over to held-out problems beyond plain RL. Reward raises a problem’s solve rate only once the model samples a success on that problem (§ 5 ). Released recipes that use the remedy, QuestA and KnowRL, reach only a little further. Their net reach is at most 0.018 0.018 (§ 4.3 ). Contributions. (1) A budget-aware split of the pass@1 gain into finishing, reliability and reach (Eqs. ( 1 )–( 5 )). Unlike pass@ k k , it separates answering in time from answering right. The split also nets reach against the reverse. (2) A read of twenty released pairs on thinking bases , the case Yue et al. (2025) leave open, at each recipe’s own training cap and the next budget above it (§ 4 ). (3) A comparison rule : compare a recipe with its base at or above its training cap. (4) A controlled probe that supplies an 8 8 B model, in five ways, the setup of physics problems its base almost never solves, and tests transfer to their text-only twins (§ 5 ). 2 Related Work What RL with verifiable rewards changes. Prior work disagrees on what outcome RL changes. None splits the measured gain into finishing and the rest. On pass@ k k curves, RL raises pass@1, but the base wins at large k k ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025b ) . RL stays within what the base can sample. Yue et al. (2025) count the problems only the RL model solves at 0 0 – 1 % 1\% on AIME24 and MATH500, at k k up to 1,024 1{,}024 . Follow-ups trace this lost coverage to hard prompts whose rare successes drop out of small sample groups ( Zhou, 2026 ) and to winner-take-all reinforcement of what the base already finds likely ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) . Others trace part of reported gains to budget mismatch and attempt inflation ( Wu et al., 2025a ; Yang & Chen, 2026 ) . Studies of derivations say RL narrows the policy where fine-tuning broadens it ( Matsutani et al., 2025 ) , acts on a few tokens where derivations branch ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and amplifies habits the base already has ( Gandhi et al., 2025 ) . Power sampling, entropy minimisation and even spurious rewards reproduce much of RL’s gain ( Karan & Du, 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2025 ) . One training example recovers most of a full data set’s gain ( Wang et al., 2025d ) . A second RL stage shortens derivations at no cost in accuracy ( Fatemi et al., 2025 ) . Both results say RL moves behaviour more than content. Prolonged training, by contrast, is reported to expand the solvable set ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Decompositions find RL improves execution within a fixed coverage ( Qin et al., 2025 ) . Fine-tuning, not RL, moves knowledge ( Wu et al., 2025c ) . All this evidence is observational: no work supplies the missing content and tests whether RL learns it. Our reliability term is the execution gain of Qin et al. (2025) with finishing removed. We compare reliability with finishing at each budget. Our reach is a term of an exact split of the pass@1 gain, counted per problem at k = 8 k=8 . The base-only count in reach controls for sampling noise. Problems only one model solves are resampled and read. Unlike budget corrections of reported gains ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , we split the gain at a fixed budget. We also read each recipe at its own cap. Objectives, samplers and replay. Other work changes how RL credits rare successes. We use one such method, replay. Pass@ k k objectives reshape the group advantage ( Chen et al., 2025d ; Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . VinePPO branches continuations to estimate credit ( Kazemnejad et al., 2024 ) . RLEP replays past successes into the group ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Replay shows what reward teaches once a success is sampled. Measuring RL on thinking models. Length and answer rate are known confounds ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2025b ; Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025 ; Hou et al., 2025 ) . For a fixed thinking model, accuracy at a cap rises with the cap ( Muennighoff et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2025 ) . Any change to derivation length therefore changes the score. We separate the two with the finishing decomposition. We also fix a held-out set before training and measure its noise floor. 3 Experimental Setup This section gives the study’s scope, the three metrics that split pass@1 under a budget (§ 3.1 ) and the protocol for reading the twenty released pairs (§ 3.2 ). Scope: thinking bases. We study thinking bases because they give RL the most to change: how long the model reasons, when it commits to an answer and how often that answer is right, not only whether it answers. A token budget makes each change visible in the score. Practice uses thinking bases too. The strongest open models on math and science, DeepSeek-R1 and its distills and Qwen3, ship in this thinking mode. Every recipe we study starts from one of them. All models studied are thinking models: the five bases (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B and 7B, Qwen3-1.7B and 4B in thinking mode, OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B), the 14 14 B and 32 32 B bases added later, and our controlled run’s Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking. Models that answer in a few hundred tokens are out of scope, except one pair read for contrast: Qwen2.5-7B and its outcome-RL version, Open-Reasoner-Zero-7B (§ 4.1 ). Scope: physics and math. To tell changed behaviour from new knowledge, we read every pair in two domains. Math is the recipes’ own domain: all twenty recipes we study train on competition math and report math results. A gain on math shows what RL buys where it was trained. A gain on physics shows what RL buys outside that domain. Physics is at most about 1 % 1\% of the RL training data of every recipe that states its mix, except ProRL v2, whose mix includes STEM. Skywork-OR1-Math-7B does not state its mix. Physics problems also need modelling, which math problems rarely exercise. A physics derivation first picks the governing principle and decides which quantities and effects matter, and only then does the algebra. A wrong setup is not repaired by careful algebra later. Once they finish at 16 16 k, the five bases are right on 85 85 – 91 % 91\% of their MATH-500 derivations but only 21 21 – 56 % 56\% of their physics ones. The modelling also makes physics derivations long, so the token budget binds more often than on math (§ 4.1 ). Test sets. Each domain has a main set and a check.
